items.stem: A team sets a Google Cloud budget of $5,000/month. What does the budget do when spend reaches it?

options.text: Sends alerts at configured thresholds; it does not stop spending
options.rationale: Correct: budgets notify at thresholds but do not cap or halt usage by themselves.
Budgets do not stop resources unless you build an automated action.

options.text: Refunds overspend to the billing account
options.rationale: There is no automatic refund for exceeding a budget.
Budgets do not block API calls.

items.explanation: Correct: Sends alerts at configured thresholds; it does not stop spending.

items.stem: Which TWO reduce cost for predictable, steady compute workloads? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Purchase committed-use discounts for the steady baseline
options.rationale: Correct: CUDs lower cost for committed, steady usage over a term.

options.text: Right-size machine types to actual utilization
options.rationale: Correct: removing over-provisioning cuts cost without hurting steady workloads.

options.text: Run the production baseline entirely on preemptible spot VMs
options.rationale: Spot VMs can be reclaimed, unsuitable for a steady production baseline.

options.text: Delete all labels to simplify billing
options.rationale: Labels aid attribution and do not reduce cost.

items.explanation: Correct: Purchase committed-use discounts for the steady baseline, Right-size machine types to actual utilization.

items.stem: Where can a team analyze detailed, line-item Google Cloud costs over time?

options.rationale: Correct: exporting billing to BigQuery enables detailed, queryable line-item analysis.
The serial console is for instance debugging, not cost analysis.
Firewall rules are network config, not cost data.
IAM manages access, not cost analysis.
